title: The Listening Choir
premise: Gideon Zhou, a meticulous property surveyor, arrives in the dying village of Hollowmere to appraise the last standing house before its final resident, elderly organist Maren Voss, signs it over to a developer. But the house answers his measurements with measurements of its own, and at dusk the church bell — melted down for scrap in 1911 — rings across the empty square. Gideon discovers the bell's sound is a choir of the drowned and disappeared, still waiting for someone to finish the song they were singing when the village flooded its own dead to hide a massacre. As Gideon documents everything in a surveyor's ledger that begins writing back, he falls for Maren's granddaughter, Ada, who came to force the sale and instead uncovers her family's role in the 1911 cover-up. In the end, Gideon must choose between delivering the appraisal that will erase Hollowmere forever and singing the forbidden last verse — an act of witness that frees the choir but condemns him to be heard by them always; Ada signs nothing, the house stands, and the bell rings only once more, gently, like a door closing.
about_author: Cyrus Quintana is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent a decade cataloguing condemned buildings across rural valleys before turning to horror. They write in longhand near water and claim never to have finished reading their own first novel.

chapters.title: The Square Footage of Silence
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. A property surveyor arrives in Hollowmere to appraise the Voss house, the last unsold parcel in a village scheduled for erasure. He measures every room twice because documentation is a kind of prayer. The emotional beat is professional calm beginning to fray: on his second pass, the hallway measures one foot longer than it did an hour ago.

chapters.title: Maren Voss Keeps Her Own Records
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. He meets Maren, ninety-one, who refuses tea but offers him a chair exactly where the light is good. She asks strange questions about what he hears. That night, from his room at the inn, Gideon hears a bell toll though the church tower has been empty since 1911. Beat: dread arriving politely.

chapters.title: Ada Comes to Close the Deal
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Maren's granddaughter arrives by bus with power of attorney and a developer's deadline, determined to sign her grandmother out of a place that is killing her slowly. She finds Gideon's survey stakes moved into patterns she almost recognizes as hymn notation. Beat: pragmatic love colliding with inherited guilt.

chapters.title: The Bell That Was Melted Down
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. In the parish archive, Gideon confirms the bell was sold for scrap in 1911, the same year eleven villagers drowned in the quarry flood — officially an accident. His ledger page for the house now contains measurements he did not take, in handwriting like wet clay. Beat: the thrill of discovery curdling.

chapters.title: What the House Appraises Back
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Ada tours the house with Gideon and watches the rooms rearrange their proportions around his tape measure, offering more space than exists. In the cellar, a wall sweats saltwater. Maren says only: 'It wants to know if you're honest.' Beat: intimacy forming between two strangers inside something hungry.

chapters.title: The Choir Under the Quarry
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Following the bell's sound, Gideon reaches the flooded quarry at night and sees figures beneath the water, mouths open, holding one sustained note. He records them on his phone; playback yields only his own breathing, then a voice counting his footsteps home. Beat: terror braided with pity.

chapters.title: Hymnal, Water-Damaged
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Ada finds Maren's mother's hymnal, its final verse torn out, the stub still damp after a century. Maren admits the torn page named the men who opened the quarry sluice gates to drown striking miners' families — names that include a Voss. Beat: loyalty to family cracking against the truth.

chapters.title: The Developer's Man
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. A smooth company representative arrives to hurry the sale, and Gideon notices the man casts no reflection in the house's dark windows — or rather, the windows reflect a different man, younger, wearing 1911 clothes. The company has been trying to buy Hollowmere for generations. Beat: conspiracy older than greed.

chapters.title: Verse One Through Verse Six
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Maren finally sings the surviving verses while Ada transcribes: a lament the drowned choir must finish to rest, but anyone who sings along joins them. Each verse sung makes the bell ring closer, louder, shaking plaster from the inn ceiling. Beat: beauty as threat; the song is a door opening by degrees.

chapters.title: The Ledger Writes Back
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Gideon's documentation becomes communion: entries appear describing events before they happen, including a line reading 'Zhou, G. — surveyed, found sufficient.' He burns the page; it reappears laminated in scale-like skin. Beat: his identity as observer collapsing into participant.

chapters.title: The Last Resident Considers Signing
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Exhausted and frightened, Maren nearly signs — the pen touches paper and every clock in the village stops mid-tick. Ada snatches the papers away and fights with her grandmother about whether staying loyal to the dead is loyalty or cowardice. Beat: love against duty, both women bleeding.

chapters.title: Drowned Men at the Doorstep
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. The choir leaves the water. Sodden figures stand in the square each dawn, one house closer to the Voss porch, singing verses one through six on repeat, patient as tide. The village dogs have all gone silent or gone. Beat: siege without walls.

chapters.title: The Company's Older Deed
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Digging through county records, Ada learns the developer's parent firm was founded by the sluice-gate owners; every purchase attempt since 1911 failed because no resident would sign. The sale isn't business — it's the perpetrators' heirs trying to legally bury the evidence. Beat: justice outside the law takes shape.

chapters.title: What Gideon Heard in Verse Four
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Transcribing Maren's singing, Gideon realizes verse four contains names — the victims naming their killers — and that the missing verse seven must contain absolution or indictment; the choir can't rest until someone worthy chooses which. He also realizes the house has been testing him all along. Beat: revelation as weight.

chapters.title: The Representative Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: POV Ada. The company man offers Ada a fortune to sign tonight, revealing he knows about the hymnal, the verse, the choir — his family has fed people to this problem for a century rather than face it. He shows her a ledger of previous surveyors who 'stayed on.' Beat: temptation wearing a nice suit.

chapters.title: Maren Remembers Singing
chapters.summary: POV Maren (first and only chapter in her voice). A memory chapter: 1954, young Maren heard the bell and sang along to verse five before her mother clamped a hand over her mouth; her brother wasn't fast enough. He has been standing in the quarry ever since, seventeen years old, waiting for her. Beat: grief as the engine of everything.

chapters.title: The Flood Comes Uphill
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Water begins seeping uphill through Hollowmere's streets, the quarry reclaiming its radius. The house floods from the top down. Gideon saves the hymnal, loses half his ledger, and understands the appraisal is nearly complete: the house is deciding what Hollowmere is worth. Beat: apocalyptic pressure, tender details amid ruin.

chapters.title: Verse Seven, Unwritten
chapters.summary: POV Ada. In the ruined chapel, Ada and Gideon find the torn page pressed behind the altar stone — blank except for a single instruction: the last verse must be composed by someone who owes the dead nothing and stays anyway. Neither of them qualifies, and both of them do. Beat: the trap and the key are the same shape.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: POV Ada. The company man forces the signing at last — Maren signs to save Ada from the rising water — and the moment ink dries, the bell rings a note that unmakes sound itself. The deed burns cold. The choir stops singing mid-verse, and the silence is worse than the song. Beat: duty fulfilled as catastrophe; the lowest point.

chapters.title: Gideon Sings
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Standing in the flooded square, Gideon improvises verse seven — not absolution, not indictment, but testimony: he reads aloud every name and fact from his surviving ledger pages, making the massacre part of the permanent record. The choir takes up his words. The water recedes toward the quarry carrying them. Beat: climax; documentation becomes literal prayer, and it works.

chapters.title: Appraised, Found Sufficient
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Dawn. The burned deed is void; the company man is gone, leaving only 1911 mud on the carpet. Maren dies peacefully that morning, hearing her brother's voice say 'finished.' Ada withdraws the sale, and the house settles into ordinary, honest dimensions. Beat: release, grief, and the quiet triumph of refusing to erase.

chapters.title: Coda: One Foot Longer
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Months later, Gideon returns to find Ada keeping the house and the archive together. His old ledger contains one new entry in his own handwriting that he doesn't remember making: coordinates, a date next spring, and the words 'they remember you kindly.' Somewhere far off, a bell rings once, gently, like a door closing. Beat: bittersweet haunting — witness is a lifelong appointment.
